questions.text: What problem do generics help solve in Rust?

answers.text: Reducing code duplication by replacing concrete types with parameters
Disabling type checking
Replacing modules
Automatically handling all errors

questions.explanation: Generics are used as abstract placeholders for types so that one implementation can work for multiple concrete cases.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Generic Types, Traits, and Lifetimes, pp. 235

questions.text: Why doesn't the simple `largest<T>` version using `>` compile for arbitrary T?

answers.text: The compiler does not know that every T supports comparison with `>`
Generic functions cannot contain loops
Slices of [T] cannot be iterated
T always means String

questions.explanation: The error shows that T must be constrained by behavior that supports comparison; this is later expressed with a trait bound.

questions.text: What does the compilation error in generic `largest<T>` demonstrate? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Not every operation can be applied to an arbitrary T
More information is needed about required type behavior
Trait bounds can express such requirements
Generics automatically provide every operator for every type

questions.explanation: The compiler needs proof that T supports the operations used; trait constraints provide that proof.

questions.text: What does `Point<T> { x: T, y: T }` mean for one instance?

answers.text: Fields x and y have the same concrete type T
x and y may have arbitrary unrelated types without more parameters
Both fields are always i32
T is chosen separately for each field

questions.explanation: A single T parameter in one instance is substituted with one concrete type for both fields.

questions.text: Which statements about `Point<T, U>` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: x can have type T
y can have a different type U
T and U may happen to be the same concrete type
Having two generic parameters requires the types to be different

questions.explanation: Separate generic parameters permit independent types but do not require them to differ.

questions.text: What roles do T and E play in `Result<T, E>`?

answers.text: T is the success-value type and E is the error type
Both are merely two names for the same type
T is an index and E is a size
They are used only at runtime and do not participate in typing

questions.explanation: Generics let the same Result enum describe many pairs of success and error types.

questions.text: Why must T be declared after `impl` in `impl<T> Point<T>`?

answers.text: So the compiler knows T is a generic parameter rather than a concrete type
To make the method asynchronous
To turn Point into an enum
Because otherwise x becomes public

questions.explanation: Declaring T on the impl introduces the parameter for the entire method block.

questions.text: Which statements about methods in `impl<T> Point<T>` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: They are available to Point instances with any concrete T unless additional constraints are given
A method can return `&T` referring to a field
T can be used in method signatures in the block
Such an impl automatically restricts Point to f32

questions.explanation: A generic `impl<T>` applies to all `Point<T>` instantiations that satisfy any stated bounds.

questions.text: What does a separate block `impl Point<f32> { ... }` mean?

answers.text: Methods in that block are available only for Point<f32>
It makes f32 a generic parameter
It adds the method to every Point<T>
It prevents Point<f32> from having other methods

questions.explanation: A concrete impl without `<T>` specializes methods for Point where T is f32.

questions.text: Suppose `Point<X1, Y1>::mixup<X2, Y2>` returns `Point<X1, Y2>`. What is the result type when it is called with `Point<i32, f64>` and `Point<&str, char>`?

answers.text: `Point<i32, char>`
`Point<&str, f64>`
`Point<i32, f64>`
`Point<&str, char>`

questions.explanation: The result takes the `x` type from `self` (`X1 = i32`) and the `y` type from the second `Point` (`Y2 = char`).

questions.text: Which statements about the performance of generics in Rust are true? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Using generics itself should not make a program slower than equivalent concrete-type code
Rust performs monomorphization at compile time
The compiler creates concrete versions of generic code for types actually used
Every generic call requires a runtime type lookup

questions.explanation: Monomorphization moves specialization of generic code to compile time.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Performance of Code Using Generics, pp. 247–248

questions.text: What is monomorphization of generics in Rust?

answers.text: Turning generic code into concrete code by substituting the types actually used
Removing all generic functions from a program
Dynamically dispatching every call
Turning a trait into a macro

questions.explanation: The compiler examines usage sites and generates specialized versions for concrete types.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Performance of Code Using Generics, pp. 247–248

questions.text: What does a trait tell the compiler?

answers.text: What common behavior a type can provide and share with other types
The exact byte size of every type
Where a module is stored in the filesystem
Which crate must be downloaded

questions.explanation: A trait describes behavior abstractly so that different types can implement it.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Traits: Defining Shared Behavior, pp. 249–254

questions.text: What can a trait definition contain in Rust? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Signatures of required methods
Methods with default implementations
Methods can use `&self`
A trait must declare data fields like a struct

questions.explanation: A trait defines methods and may provide default method bodies; it does not declare struct-style data fields.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Traits: Defining Shared Behavior, pp. 249–254

questions.text: What must a type do to implement trait `Summary` when a required method has no default implementation?

answers.text: Write `impl Summary for Type` and provide the required method implementation
Only import Summary with use
Add a summary field to the structure
Inherit from Summary with a colon on the struct

questions.explanation: A trait implementation for a type is written in a separate impl and provides the required methods.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Traits: Defining Shared Behavior, pp. 249–254

questions.text: Which benefits do traits provide as a mechanism for shared behavior? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Different types can provide the same behavioral interface
Functions can accept values of different types when they implement the required trait
Trait bounds can require specific behavior from a generic type
Traits eliminate static type checking

questions.explanation: Traits group types by behavior while preserving compile-time constraints.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Traits: Defining Shared Behavior, pp. 249–254

questions.text: What does Rust's orphan rule forbid?

answers.text: Implementing the foreign trait Display for the foreign type Vec<T> in your crate
Implementing your trait for your type
Implementing a foreign trait for your local type
Implementing your trait for a foreign type

questions.explanation: If both the trait and the type are defined outside the current crate, that implementation is forbidden.

questions.text: Why does Rust have the orphan rule?

answers.text: So different crates cannot create conflicting implementations of the same trait for the same type
To forbid all external libraries
To reduce binary size
To make traits work only with structs

questions.explanation: The rule preserves coherence; otherwise the compiler could encounter competing implementations.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Implementing a Trait on a Type, pp. 251–252

questions.text: Which statements about a trait method's default implementation are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: A trait can provide a default method body
A type can use the default without rewriting that method
A type can override the default with its own implementation
A default method cannot be called on an instance implementing the trait

questions.explanation: Defaults reduce required implementation code while preserving the ability to override behavior.

questions.text: What does a parameter `item: &impl Summary` mean?

answers.text: The function accepts a reference to a value of any type implementing Summary
The function accepts only a concrete type literally named impl
Summary becomes a field of item
The item type is determined only at runtime with no compile-time checking

questions.explanation: `impl Trait` in a parameter is concise syntax for requiring the specified trait implementation.

questions.text: Which declarations are considered equivalent for a simple single parameter? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `fn notify(item: &impl Summary)`
`fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T)`
Both restrict the accepted type through trait Summary
`fn notify<T>(item: &T)` without a bound provides the same Summary guarantee

questions.explanation: The material describes impl Trait as syntactic sugar for a simple trait bound.

questions.text: How do two parameters of type `&impl Summary` differ from two `&T` parameters with `T: Summary`?

answers.text: The first form permits different concrete types, while the second requires the same T
The first requires the same type and the second different types
They are always completely identical
The second does not check Summary

questions.explanation: One shared generic T links the types of both arguments, while separate impl Trait parameters can have different concrete types.

questions.text: What does `T: Summary + Display` allow? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Require implementation of Summary
Also require implementation of Display
Use capabilities of both traits in the function body
Mean that T must implement either Summary or Display, but not both

questions.explanation: The `+` operator combines multiple trait bounds for one type.

questions.text: Why is a `where` clause used?

answers.text: To move complex trait bounds out of the main signature and improve readability
To make trait checking dynamic
To declare a new module
To disable generic parameters

questions.explanation: `where` is an alternative syntax for placing the same constraints after the signature.

questions.text: What does return type `-> impl Summary` mean?

answers.text: The function returns some concrete type that implements Summary without naming that type in the API
The function may return any unrelated type on each call
The function returns a trait object only through Box
The function returns nothing

questions.explanation: `impl Trait` hides the concrete type from callers while preserving the Summary guarantee.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Returning Types That Implement Traits, pp. 256–258

questions.text: Which statements about return-position `impl Trait` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The concrete returned type must be the same across all branches of that definition
Calling code knows the guaranteed trait but need not know the concrete type
It is convenient for types that are difficult to write explicitly
One function can return NewsArticle in one branch and SocialPost in another only because both implement Summary

questions.explanation: The material emphasizes the one-concrete-type restriction for return-position impl Trait.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Returning Types That Implement Traits, pp. 256–258

questions.text: A function is declared as `fn make_summary(flag: bool) -> impl Summary`. Why can't it return two different concrete types from different `if` branches even if both types implement `Summary`?

answers.text: Return-position `impl Trait` must correspond to one concrete hidden type
Traits cannot be used in function return position
Conditional expressions are forbidden in functions that return `impl Trait`
A trait can be implemented by only one type

questions.explanation: `-> impl Summary` hides the concrete type from callers, but the function must still have one concrete return type across all branches.

source.locator: Chapter 10 — Returning Types That Implement Traits, pp. 256–258

questions.text: What does conditional `impl<T: Display + PartialOrd> Pair<T>` demonstrate? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Methods in the block are available only to Pair<T> where T implements both traits
Another general `impl<T>` can provide methods without these extra requirements
Bounds determine which operations are valid inside the method
Every Pair<T> automatically receives PartialOrd and Display

questions.explanation: A conditional impl adds methods only for suitable T values without changing T's own properties.

questions.text: A method on a generic type compares two values with `>` and then formats the selected value with `{}`. Which trait bounds are required for that method?

answers.text: `PartialOrd + Display`
Only `Clone`
Only `Debug`
`Iterator + IntoIterator`

questions.explanation: `PartialOrd` is needed for comparison with `>`, while `Display` is needed for `{}` formatting.

questions.text: Which statements about blanket implementations are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: A trait can be implemented for any type satisfying a specified bound
Such broad implementations are widely used in the standard library
An example is ToString for types implementing Display
A blanket implementation means implementing a trait only for one preselected type

questions.explanation: A blanket impl extends an implementation to an entire set of types satisfying a condition.

questions.text: How do generics and trait bounds complement each other? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Generics let one body of code work with different types
Trait bounds constrain generic types to required behavior
The compiler checks these requirements statically
Generic code always requires dynamic type checking

questions.explanation: Generics provide reuse while traits formulate safe constraints on permitted types.

questions.text: What happens if a type that does not implement Summary is passed to `notify(item: &impl Summary)`?

answers.text: The code does not compile
The function runs and skips summarize
Summary is automatically added to the type
Only a runtime warning is produced

questions.text: Which methods can safely be called on a parameter of type `&impl Summary` inside the function? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Methods provided by trait Summary
Methods made available by additional bounds
`summarize`, if it is part of Summary
Any arbitrary method of any Rust type without bounds

questions.explanation: A generic function body can rely only on behavior guaranteed by its bounds.
